claims.text: Successful nanoparticle homogenization is governed by synchronized reduction of all noble-metal precursors.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation kinetically freezes a high-entropy state before thermodynamically driven segregation occurs.
The proposed precursor solution contains multiple noble-metal salts, a reducing agent, and surface-stabilizing ligands in an inert solvent.
The noble-metal salts have inherently different reduction potentials.
A rapid pulsed thermal treatment can induce near-instantaneous reduction of all metal precursors.
A short high-temperature pulse followed by rapid quenching minimizes dwell time at intermediate reduction stages.
The treatment transiently forms amorphous alloy clusters.
The amorphous alloy clusters rapidly crystallize into uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
Rapid cluster crystallization preserves high surface-area exposure.
Synchronizing precursor-reduction kinetics avoids sequential or preferential reduction.
Sequential or preferential reduction leads to atomic segregation and phase separation.
The rapid pulse limits thermodynamically driven segregation and favors homogeneous alloy formation.
Relative to a slow thermal ramp, pulsed treatment will produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to a slow thermal ramp, pulsed treatment will produce a more controlled and uniform particle morphology.
Uniform elemental distribution and morphology ensure a high density of surface-active sites.
A slow thermal ramp causes staggered reduction kinetics.
Staggered reduction under a slow ramp produces phase-separated or compositionally segregated particles with irregular morphologies.
The hypothesis applies to noble-metal systems containing at least five elements when their kinetic differences can be overcome by a rapid thermal pulse.
The hypothesis may fail when precursor-reduction kinetics are too disparate or ligands drastically alter reduction behavior.
The optimal pulse temperature, duration, and quenching rate depend on the metal combination and precursor chemistry.
